concepts.def: System of legal racial segregation built by the National Party after its 1948 election victory, classifying South Africans by race and separating them in housing, education and public life.
Law classifying every South African by racial group — White, Coloured, Indian or Black African — providing the administrative foundation for all other apartheid legislation.
Laws requiring Black South Africans to carry passbooks controlling where they could live, work and travel; resistance to the passes sparked major protest campaigns.
On 21 March 1960 police opened fire on an anti-pass-law crowd at Sharpeville, killing 69 people; the government then banned the ANC and PAC.
Student protests beginning on 16 June 1976 against compulsory teaching in Afrikaans; police shootings of schoolchildren triggered nationwide unrest and international outrage.
ANC leader sentenced to life imprisonment at the Rivonia Trial in 1964, released in 1990, and elected South Africa's first Black president in the 1994 election.

Depth Study: South Africa c1940-c1994 — a core area of GCSE History.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Depth Study: South Africa c1940-c1994 brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

mcqs.q: In which year did the National Party win power and begin building apartheid?
What happened at Sharpeville on 21 March 1960?
options: Police fired on an anti-pass-law crowd, killing 69 people
Nelson Mandela was released from prison
The first democratic election was held
Students protested against teaching in Afrikaans

mcqs.q: Why was the Soweto Uprising of 1976 significant?
options: A student protest against compulsory Afrikaans grew into nationwide resistance to apartheid
It ended apartheid immediately
It was the first time the ANC was banned
It led directly to Mandela's release that same year

mcqs.q: Who became South Africa's first Black president in 1994?
options: Desmond Tutu
F.W. de Klerk
Nelson Mandela
Steve Biko

mcqs.q: Why did apartheid end in the early 1990s?
options: A combination of internal resistance, international sanctions and economic pressure, and negotiations between de Klerk's government and Mandela's ANC produced a negotiated settlement and the 1994 election.
He was imprisoned for organising the Soweto Uprising.
The United Nations voted to abolish apartheid and forced South Africa to comply.
Apartheid ended when Britain resumed direct rule over South Africa in 1990.

mcqs.q: What was the policy of 'separate development' (the Bantustans)?
options: The Bantustans were whites-only farming districts near Cape Town.
Apartheid ended when Britain resumed direct rule over South Africa in 1990.
The Bantustans were genuinely independent countries recognised by the international community.
Black South Africans were assigned to ethnic 'homelands' and stripped of South African citizenship, which the government used to justify excluding them from political rights.

mcqs.q: Why was Nelson Mandela imprisoned in 1964?
options: He was imprisoned simply for being a member of the ANC and making speeches.
He was imprisoned for organising the Soweto Uprising.
He was convicted of sabotage at the Rivonia Trial for his role in Umkhonto we Sizwe's armed campaign against the apartheid state.
Apartheid ended when Britain resumed direct rule over South Africa in 1990.
